case.limits: It construes one state statute. It travels only as far as BIPA's reach and the growing family of statutes modelled on it, and federal courts still filter such claims through Article III standing.
case.holding: A person whose biometric data is collected in violation of BIPA is aggrieved and may sue without alleging any further injury. The statutory violation itself is the harm.
case.case_name: Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entertainment Corp.

live_cases.name: Miller v. Clearview AI "Artificial Intelligence" Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The decision that armed BIPA. Face-recognition and voice-model litigation against AI companies proceeds on Rosenbach's rule that collection without the required notice and consent is actionable per se, which is why Illinois is where biometric AI cases are filed and settled at nine and ten figures.

reading.body:
Rosenbach v. Six Flags, a 2019 Illinois Supreme Court case holding that a BIPA violation is itself the harm without any further injury required, is cited by plaintiffs in both Clearview AI lawsuits tracked here, the same two cases as Patel v. Facebook.

The record states plainly that this decision is why Illinois is where biometric AI cases are filed and settled at nine and ten figures, which is a specific, quantified consequence rather than a general legal principle, and it is the only precedent in this collection with that kind of stated financial stakes attached to it.

Its own limit is jurisdictional rather than doctrinal. It construes one state statute, and travels only as far as BIPA and the family of statutes modeled on it, while federal courts still filter such claims through separate Article III standing analysis, the same limit noted in the companion Patel case.
